card.h1: The efficiency of agricultural machinery: why utilization beats horsepower
A machine that sits idle is more expensive than no machine at all

ul.li: Farmers judge alsintan by purchase price and engine power. Both are the wrong number.
Ownership cost is fixed per year and falls per hectare only as use rises
The same transplanter can cost Rp 1,023,000 or Rp 666,000 per hectare — identical machine, different calendar
This deck builds the arithmetic that separates the two, then walks one worked case end to end

card.h1: "Efficiency" hides three separate questions — measure all three

ul.li: Field efficiency: what share of field time is actual work, not turning, refilling or waiting
Cost efficiency: rupiah per hectare, fixed plus variable, at your real annual use
Loss and labor efficiency: grain saved and workdays released per hectare
A machine can score well on one and fail on another — high capacity, chronically underused

card.h1: Field capacity: the one formula the rest of the deck rests on

ul.li: Theoretical field capacity = speed (km/h) × working width (m) ÷ 10, in ha/hour
Effective field capacity = theoretical × field efficiency; field efficiency covers headland turns, refuelling, refilling
Worked example: a subsoiler at 5 km/h, 2 m spacing, 17% of time lost to turning and refuelling → efficiency 0.83 → 5 × 2 × 0.83 = 8.3 ha per 10-hour day
Typical field efficiencies: plows 78–85%, tandem disk ~80–83%, fertilizer spreader ~70%

card.h1: A measured Indonesian machine: the Indo Jarwo transplanter at 86%

ul.li: Field test in Pinrang, South Sulawesi, on 10 × 10 m plots at three speeds
Best working speed 1.52 km/h; theoretical capacity 0.14 ha/h; effective capacity 0.12 ha/h
Field efficiency = 0.12 ÷ 0.14 = 86%, or 8.33 hours to plant one hectare
A BBP Mektan manual transplanter measured separately reached 86.79%, with 4.2% of time lost
Reproduce it on your own plot: time one pass, measure the width, count the turns

card.h1: Where the missing 14% goes — and which parts you can buy back

ul.li: Headland turning: the largest single loss; falls with longer runs and squarer plots
Refilling seedling trays or tanks: reduced by staging supplies at the headland, not the road
Adjustment and clearing blockages: operator skill, directly trainable
Transport between fragmented plots: not field time at all, but it eats the working day
Plot geometry and logistics, not the engine, set most of this number

card.h1: Five stages of use, each with its own efficiency trap

ol.li: Land preparation — hand tractor; output up to 15× manual hoeing in measured trials
Planting — transplanter; manual seeding-to-planting needs 32.79 male and 23.79 female hours per hectare against 18.67 male hours mechanized
Crop care — power weeder, sprayer; ~10× manual weeding output
Harvest — combine harvester; three workers, about five hours per hectare
Post-harvest — thresher and dryer; thresher output ~17× manual

card.h1: Choosing the machine: six checks before the purchase order

ul.li: Match power to the heaviest task, not the average one; undersized units finish late and wear fast
Plot size and shape: small fragmented plots cap field efficiency whatever the machine costs
Soil and water condition: puddled paddy, dry upland and peat demand different traction
Annual area available: compare it to the break-even area before committing
Service, spare parts and operator skill within reach of the village
Custom-hire alternative: if the local rate beats your cost per hectare, hire instead of buy

card.h1: Cost splits in two, and only one half responds to use

ul.li: Fixed (ownership): depreciation, interest, insurance, housing — unchanged whether you run 5 ha or 50
Straight-line depreciation = (purchase price − salvage value) ÷ years of optimal life
Variable (operating): fuel, lubricant, repairs, operator wages — roughly constant per hectare
So cost per hectare = (annual fixed ÷ hectares worked) + variable per hectare
The first term is the whole argument: it is a division, and hectares are the denominator

card.h1: Break-even area: the number that decides buy or hire

ul.li: Break-even area = annual fixed cost ÷ (custom rate − variable cost per hectare)
Below it, owning costs more per hectare than paying someone else
Measured case: a modified manual transplanter in Sijunjung, West Sumatra cost Rp 325,057/ha against Rp 653,343/ha for manual planting, with a break-even of 13.46 ha per year
Cheap machine, low break-even. A four-wheel combine shifts that threshold by an order of magnitude

card.h1: Harvest loss is efficiency you can weigh in the sack

ul.li: In Banten, matched-sample analysis found combine harvesters cut harvest loss by 200.39 kg per hectare, about 3.52% of yield
In Sumbawa, losses averaged 0.43%/ha with a combine against 1.03%/ha manually, and production cost Rp 9.33 million/ha against Rp 11.27 million/ha
A Kubota DC70 Plus trial in North Sulawesi measured total loss of 4.9% — 4.7% scattered during cutting alone
Read the gap carefully: figures differ because studies count different losses. Define what you measure before you compare machines

card.h1: Seven indicators worth tracking every season

ul.li: Effective field capacity (ha/hour) — actual area ÷ actual field hours
Field efficiency (%) — effective ÷ theoretical capacity
Utilization (ha/year) — compare directly against break-even area
Cost per hectare (Rp) — fixed plus variable, recalculated annually
Harvest or process loss (%) — weighed, not estimated
Fuel per hectare (litres) — the earliest warning of a maintenance problem
Downtime (% of scheduled days) — where the season is actually lost

card.h1: Case study: UPJA Tani Makmur buys a transplanter

li.b: Illustrative example — a fictional farmer-group service unit, figures constructed to be reproducible, not drawn from a real cooperative

ul.li: Machine Rp 75,000,000; 8-year life; 10% salvage → depreciation Rp 8,437,500/year
Interest at 8% on average investment of Rp 41,250,000 → Rp 3,300,000; housing and insurance Rp 1,125,000
Annual fixed cost = Rp 12,862,500. Variable cost (fuel, oil, two operators, repairs) = Rp 380,000/ha
Local custom planting rate: Rp 700,000/ha → break-even = 12,862,500 ÷ (700,000 − 380,000) = 40.2 ha/year
Year one they served 20 ha. Cost per hectare: Rp 1,023,000 — well above the rate they charged

card.h1: The calendar, not the machine, was the binding constraint

ul.li: At 0.12 ha/h and 6 working hours a day, the machine plants 0.72 ha/day
One village's 20-day planting window, two seasons: 0.72 × 20 × 2 = 28.8 ha/year ceiling — below break-even before a single delay
The fix was scheduling, not equipment: staggered planting dates across three neighbouring villages widened the window to 25 days and justified 8-hour days
New ceiling: 0.96 × 25 × 2 = 48 ha/year. At 45 ha served, cost falls to Rp 666,000/ha — now under the Rp 700,000 rate
No new horsepower was purchased. The gain came entirely from access to more days

card.h1: Five strategies, in order of return per rupiah spent

ul.li: Raise utilization first. Shared UPJA service across villages with staggered planting turns fixed cost into a smaller divisor
Train operators. Turning discipline and quick blockage clearing move field efficiency several points at near-zero cost
Preventive maintenance. Scheduled servicing protects the working days that break-even depends on
Right-size, don't over-size. Extra capacity that the calendar cannot use is pure fixed cost
Measure and record. Effective field capacity from your own logbook beats any brochure figure

card.h1: What to take back to the field

ul.li: Efficiency is a ratio you compute, not a quality the machine possesses
Field efficiency of 80–86% is realistic and measurable; the missing share is mostly geometry and logistics
Cost per hectare is governed by annual use; break-even area is the single decisive figure before buying
Mechanization pays in loss avoided and labour released, not only in speed
First action: time one pass, weigh one loss sample, and compare your cost per hectare to the local custom rate

brief.instruction: Technical and plain, written for agricultural engineering students, extension officers and farmer-group decision-makers. Sentence case. Short declarative sentences with exact units and figures; state the finding rather than the topic. About 55 words per slide; the template holds median 52.5, p90 78, so budget 55 a slide and go to 78 only on a deliberately text-only slide such as the cost-structure or case-study cards. Every rupiah figure carries its unit and basis (per hectare, per year). Keep arithmetic visible: show the inputs, the operation and the result on the same line so a reader can reproduce it, e.g. "12,862,500 ÷ (700,000 − 380,000) = 40.2 ha/year". Vary sentence and paragraph length. Never use the "Bold term: explanation" pattern as a whole-slide format — the lead-in labels in this outline are deliberate and limited, so keep at least one slide in each pair free of them. No signposting phrases, no sweeping openers, no inspirational closers, no "not just X — it's Y" constructions, no em dashes. Indonesian terms (alsintan, UPJA, jajar legowo) appear in English prose with a brief gloss on first use.

White background with red accents throughout: the template's red rules, chart series and accent marks carry the emphasis against a clean white ground. Restrained and technical, closer to an engineering training deck than a marketing piece. Imagery is documentary photography of real field work: hand tractors in puddled paddy, a rice transplanter mid-pass with the operator walking behind, a combine harvester working a ripe field, grain being weighed and sacked, a mechanic servicing an engine. People at work, never posed, natural directional light. Avoid stock-looking smiling farmers and avoid any imagery implying a specific real cooperative or brand. Give the numeric slides real evidence furniture rather than photographs: the formula slide should set the field-capacity equation as a boxed expression with a symbol key; the break-even slide takes the supplied cost-curve chart with the crossing point marked in red; the indicators slide is a ruled table of indicator, unit and how to measure it; the five stages slide uses the template's arrow-banner sequence. The two case-study slides are the deck's peak: give the first a substantial cost ledger and the second a clear before-and-after of the annual ceiling (28.8 ha against 48 ha) so the jump is visible without reading the body copy. The opening cost contrast (Rp 1,023,000 against Rp 666,000 per hectare) deserves oversized figures.

No source document, client data or company assets were supplied for this deck; it is built from published field research plus one constructed example. UPJA Tani Makmur is fictional. Its label as an illustrative example must appear on the first case-study slide exactly as written in the outline and must not be dropped or softened. Do not add a logo, photograph, location detail, quotation or testimonial that would imply the cooperative, its members or its results are real. All cited figures (Pinrang transplanter capacity, Sijunjung break-even, Banten and Sumbawa harvest losses, Kubota DC70 trial, field-efficiency tables) come from the referenced studies and must be reproduced exactly as written, with their units and their qualifiers intact. Do not round them, merge them, or generalize a single-site result into a national claim. The constructed arithmetic in the case study is internally consistent; do not alter any input value, because every downstream figure depends on it. Invent no additional statistics, prices, yields or outcomes anywhere in the deck.
